headline: Where Did the Fluke Go? Follow the Cool Water to the Inlets
subhead: Warm bay water is pushing the fluke program toward Absecon and Great Egg while the first real signs of the fall turn start to show at the inlet mouths.
body_markdown:
The question I've gotten more than any other this week, from the rail at the Brigantine ramp to the phone calls after Sunday service, is some version of: "Where'd the fluke go?" Fair question for late August. The answer is the same lesson I've been teaching this beat for thirty years — when the back bay water gets warm and thin on oxygen, the fluke don't disappear, they relocate. Right now that means the mud flats and sod banks in the upper reaches of Absecon and Great Egg are fishing softer than they were three weeks ago, while the channel edges tight to the inlet mouths and the ocean-front structure off Ocean City and Townsends are holding up better.

That's the pattern we flagged coming — fluke staying catchable on structure and in the deeper channels through September rather than falling off a cliff, and that's exactly what the fleet is finding. It's not a bell-ringer bite anywhere right now, but it's a fair one if you fish the right water on the right stage of tide. Best producers this week have been white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the sod bank channels dump into the main inlet current — the last two hours of the outgoing at Great Egg has been the most consistent window, with fish stacking on that seam where warm bay water meets the cooler, moving inlet water. A few boats working bucktail-and-Gulp combos in 12 to 18 feet off the Rt. 52 causeway rubble in Ocean City have picked at keeper-class fish in that same 18 to 22 inch class, nothing spectacular in size, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you're patient and keep the boat moving.

Bluefish have been the most dependable predator in the mix, and that tracks with what the bait is doing. Bunker pods have been building along the beachfront from Brigantine down through Stone Harbor, and wherever those schools bunch up tight, the blues are on them — snapping bunker chunks and casting big straight-tail plastics into the melee has been producing fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, with some better ones mixed in off the Ocean City pier and the north end of Townsends Inlet on the last of the ebb. That's the call we made last week — bluefish activity tracking bunker density — and it's holding true almost to the letter. Watch those bunker schools closely over the next several days, because wherever they concentrate tight against the beach or stack up in the inlet mouths, that's your tell for the first real striper activity of the fall.

Speaking of stripers, there's finally something to write about there. It's early and it's not a blitz by any stretch, but a handful of school bass in the mid-20-inch range have started showing at first light around the Absecon Inlet rocks and the Great Egg jetty, working the bunker pods on the last hour of the incoming. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounces, cast up-current and swung through the seam, have taken a few. Don't build a trip around it yet — the real push is still a week or two off, tied to bait density concentrating further as the moon builds toward full and tidal flow strengthens — but it's worth a rod in the spread if you're already out there working blues or fluke.

Kingfish have been scattered but present in the surf from Ocean City down to Stone Harbor, biting best on bloodworms and Fishbites fished on a high-low rig in the wash during the middle of the outgoing tide, particularly in that sandy trough water that holds after a period of onshore wind. Weakfish have been quiet — a few reports of fish in the 16 to 18 inch range coming from the deeper holes inside Great Egg on soft plastics fished after dark, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. Triggerfish are showing up as a bonus around the Townsends Inlet jetty rocks and the Ocean City inlet structure, taking small pieces of clam or green crab fished tight to the rip-rap on light tackle — fun catch, not a program to plan around.

The bigger story for the week ahead is the warm-water visitors starting to work their way down the coast. With the same warm filament that's been pushing bonito and false albacore into play further north continuing to extend its influence south, the reef structure and open beachfront from Absecon to Stone Harbor is worth watching closely over the next several days — that's the call we made, and the ingredients are lining up. If that warm water holds and the bait stays thick along the beach, don't be surprised if the first bonito of the season show up working bait pods within casting range of the surf.

Looking at the next 72 hours: expect the fluke bite to hold in that fair-but-fishable range, best worked on the outgoing at the inlet channel edges rather than the upper bay flats. The bluefish should stay steady as long as bunker holds along the beach. The moon building toward full over the next week should start concentrating bait tighter into the inlet mouths, and that's the signal to watch for the striper pattern to take its next step. If you've only got one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the outgoing at Great Egg or Absecon — that's where the classroom says to be right now.
